expectedText:
MEDI-CAL ESTATE RECOVERY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Pat Morgan · March 15, 2026

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet summarizes California's Medi-Cal Estate Recovery Program under Welfare and Institutions Code Section 14009.5, as it applies to the estate of Pat Morgan (date of death: March 15, 2026; estimated estate value: Real property and financial accounts with an estimated total value of $650,000). It states what the law provides in general; it does not calculate whether the California Department of Health Care Services (DHCS) has asserted, or will assert, a claim against this specific estate, and it is not a substitute for DHCS's own accounting of amounts it may claim.

WHAT CAN TRIGGER A RECOVERY CLAIM
Under Welfare and Institutions Code Section 14009.5, DHCS may claim against the estate of a deceased Medi-Cal member, or against a recipient of that decedent's property by distribution, for an amount equal to the Medi-Cal payments made for that person's health care services or the value of the property received, whichever is less. That claim is authorized only in two circumstances: against the real property of a Medi-Cal member of any age who was an inpatient in a nursing facility and met specified federal Medicaid eligibility criteria, or where the decedent was 55 years of age or older when the individual received the health care services being recovered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Notwithstanding any other provision of this chapter, the department shall claim against the estate of the decedent, or against any recipient of the property of that decedent by distribution, an amount equal to the payments for the health care services received or the value of the property received by any recipient from the decedent by distribution, whichever is less, only in either of the following circumstances:"
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(b) (California Legislative Information text), Welfare and Institutions Code, Medi-Cal estate recovery, claim amount and triggers (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  "(1) Against the real property of a Medi-Cal member of any age who meets the criteria in Section 1396p(a)(1)(B) of Title 42 of the United States Code and who was or is an inpatient in a nursing facility in accordance with Section 1396p(b)(1)(A) of Title 42 of the United States Code."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), nursing-facility inpatient trigger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  "(2) (A) The decedent was 55 years of age or older when the individual received health care services."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(b)(2)(A) (California Legislative Information text), age-55-or-older trigger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  Known gap: The statute limits recovery to these two triggers, but whether a specific person's Medi-Cal benefits meet the federal 'health care services' definition subject to recovery, or whether a person met the nursing-facility criteria the statute cross-references in federal law, are determinations this document does not make for a particular estate.

RECOVERY IS LIMITED TO THE PROBATE ESTATE
For an individual who dies on or after January 1, 2017, Section 14009.5 defines 'estate' for Medi-Cal recovery purposes as only the real and personal property and other assets in the decedent's probate estate that federal law requires be subject to a claim for recovery. Before that date, California's Medi-Cal estate recovery statute defined 'estate' more broadly, and DHCS could reach some property that passed outside of probate, such as property held in joint tenancy, assets held in a revocable living trust, or assets passing by a beneficiary designation. This narrowing took effect through a 2016 amendment (SB 833, Stats. 2016, ch. 30), whose own statement of legislative intent describes limiting Medi-Cal estate recovery to only what federal law requires and limiting the definition of 'estate' accordingly.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(3) “Estate” means all real and personal property and other assets in the individual’s probate estate that are required to be subject to a claim for recovery pursuant to Section 1396p(b)(4)(A) of Title 42 of the United States Code."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(f)(3) (California Legislative Information text), current statutory definition of 'estate,' limited to the probate estate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  "(1) Limit Medi-Cal estate recovery only for those services required to be collected under federal law."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(a)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text), stated legislative intent to narrow recovery and the 'estate' definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  "(2) Limit the definition of “estate” to include only the real and personal property and other assets required to be collected under federal law."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), stated legislative intent to narrow the 'estate' definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  "The amendments made to this section by the act that added this subdivision shall apply only to individuals who die on or after January 1, 2017."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(g) (California Legislative Information text), effective date of the narrower definition (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  Known gap: This document's description of the pre-2017 rule (that it reached certain non-probate transfers such as joint tenancy property, living trust assets, and beneficiary designations) reflects the current statute's own statement of what the 2016 amendment was intended to change, and is consistent with how this amendment is widely described in secondary legal sources; this session did not independently fetch and diff the pre-amendment text of Section 14009.5 against the current text, so the exact wording and full scope of the prior, broader 'estate' definition is not verified word-for-word against primary-source text from that era.

EXEMPTION FOR A SURVIVING SPOUSE OR MINOR/DISABLED CHILD
Under the age-55-or-older recovery trigger, Section 14009.5 bars DHCS from claiming against the estate when the decedent is survived by a spouse or registered domestic partner, by a child who is under 21 years of age, or by a child who is blind or disabled within the meaning of the federal Supplemental Security Income disability standard. The statute separately states that prohibiting recovery from the estate of a deceased Medi-Cal member survived by a spouse or registered domestic partner was itself one of the stated purposes of the amendment that added this framework.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(B) The department shall not claim under this paragraph when there is any of the following: (i) A surviving spouse or surviving registered domestic partner. (ii) A surviving child who is under 21 years of age. (iii) A surviving child who is blind or disabled, within the meaning of Section 1614 of the federal Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. Sec. 1382c)."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(b)(2)(B) (California Legislative Information text), surviving spouse, domestic partner, and child exceptions to the age-55 trigger (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  "(4) Prohibit recovery from the estate of a deceased Medi-Cal member who is survived by a spouse or registered domestic partner."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), stated legislative intent to prohibit recovery when survived by a spouse or domestic partner (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  Known gap: This bar applies by its own terms to the age-55-or-older trigger in subdivision (b)(2); the statute's separate nursing-facility-inpatient trigger in subdivision (b)(1) is not made subject to this same list of surviving-spouse-or-child exceptions by its own text. This document does not resolve how DHCS treats an estate where both triggers could otherwise apply.

HARDSHIP WAIVER AND THE MODEST-VALUE HOMESTEAD
Apart from the surviving-spouse-or-child limitation, Section 14009.5 separately requires DHCS to waive its claim, in whole or in part, if enforcing it would cause substantial hardship to other dependents, heirs, or survivors of the person whose estate is subject to the claim. In deciding whether that substantial hardship exists, DHCS must, subject to federal approval, waive its claim when the estate being recovered from is a 'homestead of modest value' — a home whose fair market value is 50 percent or less of the average price of homes in the county where it is located, valued as of the decedent's date of death. The statute directs DHCS to notify individuals of this waiver provision and of the opportunity for a hearing to establish that a waiver should be granted.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "(1) The department shall waive its claim, in whole or in part, if it determines that enforcement of the claim would result in substantial hardship to other dependents, heirs, or survivors of the individual against whose estate the claim exists."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(c)(1) (California Legislative Information text), mandatory substantial-hardship waiver (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  "(2) In determining the existence of substantial hardship, in addition to other factors considered by the department consistent with federal law and guidance, the department shall, subject to federal approval, waive its claim when the estate subject to recovery is a homestead of modest value."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(c)(2) (California Legislative Information text), mandatory waiver for a homestead of modest value (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  "“Homestead of modest value” means a home whose fair market value is 50 percent or less of the average price of homes in the county where the homestead is located, as of the date of the decedent’s death."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(f)(5) (California Legislative Information text), definition of 'homestead of modest value' (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  "(3) The department shall notify individuals of the waiver provision and the opportunity for a hearing to establish that a waiver should be granted."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(c)(3) (California Legislative Information text), notice of the waiver provision and hearing opportunity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  Known gap: The statute states the substantial-hardship standard and the homestead-of-modest-value definition, and directs DHCS to give notice of the waiver opportunity, but it does not itself set out the application procedure, required forms, or evidentiary showing DHCS uses to decide a hardship-waiver request — those mechanics are left to DHCS regulations and administrative guidance. This session attempted to reach dhcs.ca.gov directly for that procedural detail; the requests returned only an automated bot-detection challenge page (an Incapsula interstitial) rather than substantive content, so no DHCS regulatory or procedural detail beyond this statute's own text could be independently verified this session.

RIGHT TO REQUEST AN ACCOUNTING WHILE THE MEMBER IS LIVING
Section 14009.5 gives a current or former Medi-Cal member, or that member's authorized representative, the right to request from DHCS a statement of the Medi-Cal expenses that may be recoverable under this section through the date of the request. DHCS may respond within 90 days of a complete request and may charge a fee of up to five dollars, once per calendar year, for a member who was 55 or older when receiving the services, or who is a permanently institutionalized inpatient in a nursing facility, intermediate care facility for the intellectually disabled, or other medical institution.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The department shall provide a current or former member, or his or her authorized representative designated under Section 14014.5, upon request, a copy of the amount of Medi-Cal expenses that may be recoverable under this section through the date of the request."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(e)(1) (California Legislative Information text), member's right to request an accounting of recoverable expenses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  "(4) Upon receiving a request for the information described in paragraph (1) and all necessary supporting documentation, the department shall provide the information requested within 90 days after receipt of the request."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 14009.5(e)(4) (California Legislative Information text), 90-day response deadline (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=14009.5.)
  Known gap: This request right, as the statute states it, belongs to the living member or their authorized representative. The statute does not describe a parallel mechanism by which an estate's personal representative can request this same accounting after the member has died, and this document does not assume one exists.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Prepared by Jordan T. Reyes regarding the estate of Pat Morgan (date of death: March 15, 2026; estimated estate value: Real property and financial accounts with an estimated total value of $650,000).

Signed: _______________________________
Date: September 1, 2026
Location: Oakland, California
